                    ### Question
                    A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a 2-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased appetite. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F). Abdominal examination shows tenderness to palpation with guarding in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 12,600/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Bacterial mesenteric lymphadenitis
opb. Pseudomembranous plaque formation in the colon
opc. Diverticular inflammation
opd. Congenital anomaly of the omphalomesenteric duct
ope. Lymphatic tissue hyperplasia

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 15-year-old girl presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, and right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding, alongside an elevated leukocyte count. These symptoms are suggestive of an acute abdominal process, likely due to infection or inflammation. Bacterial mesenteric lymphadenitis is a common cause of such symptoms in this age group, particularly following viral infections or gastroenteritis. Pseudomembranous colitis is less likely given the absence of antibiotic history, and diverticular inflammation is rare in this demographic. Congenital anomalies of the omphalomesenteric duct are also uncommon. Lymphatic tissue hyperplasia could be a consideration but is not the most typical presentation. Therefore, bacterial mesenteric lymphadenitis is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition, supported by the clinical presentation and age group.
